# Filtering by file type

ripgrep ships with a set of named file types. A type is a name plus a list of
file name globs, and it saves you from writing `-g '*.[ch]pp' -g '*.cc' -g
'*.hh'` for the ninth time. Four flags cover everything you'll do with them.

## Search one type

`-t/--type` limits the search to files matching a type:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

Pass the flag again for each additional type. There's no comma list, so one
type per flag:

```
$ rg -tpy -tjs 'def '
```

The name can be attached to the short flag (`-trust`) or given separately
(`--type rust`). Name a type ripgrep doesn't know and it says so and stops:
`rg: unrecognized file type: nosuchtype`.

## Skip a type

`-T/--type-not` is the inverse. It excludes files matching a type and leaves
everything else searchable:

```
$ rg clap -Trust
```

The difference matters. As soon as you use one `-t`, every file that doesn't
match a selected type is excluded. `-T` on its own excludes only what you
named.

## Order decides

`-t` and `-T` accumulate in the order you write them, and when both cover the
same file, the last one wins. So `rg -trust -Trust needle` searches nothing,
while `rg -Trust -trust needle` searches your Rust files. Write the broad flag
first and the exception after it.

Types are the weakest of ripgrep's filters. Both `-g/--glob` and any rule in a
`.gitignore` or `.ignore` file take precedence, so this searches Rust files in
spite of the `-T`:

```
$ rg -Trust -g '*.rs' needle
```

## See the definitions

`--type-list` prints every type and its globs, one per line, name first, then a
colon and a comma-delimited list. It prints and exits without searching. Pipe
it back through ripgrep when you want one entry:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, [Gg][Nn][Uu]makefile, [Gg][Nn][Uu]makefile.am, ...
```

Run this before you guess at a name. The built-in types generally track well
known public formats, and the set changes between releases.

## Define your own

`--type-add` takes a `name:glob` pair and defines a new type or extends an
existing one. Only one glob per flag, so either repeat the flag or use a brace
alternation:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Both commands define a `web` type and then search it. Your new type shows up in
`rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list` alongside the built-in ones.

A type can also be built from other types with the `include` directive, which
copies their globs in:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc needle
```

The types you include must already be defined, so a bare `--type-add
'src:include:foo'` fails with `rg: invalid definition` unless `foo` was defined
earlier on the same command line. Adding globs to `src` afterwards works fine:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' needle
```

Names must consist only of Unicode letters or numbers. `my-type` is rejected,
and `all` is reserved.

By default a `--type-add` glob joins the type's existing globs. To replace a
definition instead, clear it first with `--type-clear`, then add:

```
$ rg --type-clear py --type-add 'py:*.pyx' --type-list | rg '^py:'
py: *.pyx
```

## Making a type stick

`--type-add` and `--type-clear` apply to the current command only. Nothing is
saved. If you want a type everywhere, use a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or put it in your configuration file, which ripgrep reads from the path in
`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`. Flags with values go on one line with an `=`, or across
two lines:

```
# Add my 'web' type.
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## What type globs match

A type glob is tested against the file name alone, never the full path.
`--type-add 'web:src/*.js'` matches nothing. Reach for `-g 'src/*.js'` when you
want to filter on path shape.

Type filters also don't apply to directories, so a directory named `old.rs`
doesn't get pulled in by `-trust` or skipped by `-Trust`. Only the files inside
it are judged, on their own names.

This is also why `rg -tsh` misses an extensionless shell script. The `sh` type's
globs cover `*.sh`, `.bashrc`, `profile` and friends, but nothing that has no
extension and no known name.

## The special `all` type

`--type=all` behaves as if you'd passed `-t` for every type, including your
custom ones. That's whitelist mode: ripgrep searches only files it recognizes.

`--type-not=all` is blacklist mode. It searches only the files no type claims,
which is a quick way to find the extensionless scripts, `LICENSE` files and odd
data your other searches keep missing.
